transcript.text: Moved house today, plugged the fridge freezer in as soon as we got it in and 3 hours later it's still not cold and gurgling a lot. Have the movers broken it?

Probably not. A fridge freezer starting from room temperature usually needs 6 to 12 hours to get the fridge properly cold, and the freezer can take up to 24 hours to reach -18°C. The gurgling and bubbling is also normal. That's the refrigerant moving round the pipes, and it's often louder for the first day after a move while everything settles. The one thing that matters is how it travelled. If it was laid on its side or back, the compressor oil can run into the cooling pipes. Running it straight away can stop it cooling properly and, in the worst case, damage the compressor. 1. If it was laid down at any point, switch it off now. Let it stand upright for several hours, ideally up to 24, then switch it back on. If it stayed upright the whole way, leave it running.
2. Check the temperature control hasn't been knocked during the move. Aim for about 3–5°C in the fridge and -18°C in the freezer, with no holiday or eco mode on.
3. Make sure it has a few centimetres of space at the back and sides so it can get rid of heat.
4. Listen for a low steady hum from the bottom at the back, and feel whether the sides or back are warm. That means the compressor is running and it's doing its job. A click every few minutes with no cooling, or total silence, would be worth telling me about. Then keep the doors shut and don't load food until it's properly cold, ideally tomorrow. Warm food slows it down a lot. If it's still not cold after a full 24 hours of running (after standing first, if it was laid down), that's when it starts to look like a real fault rather than settling. Let me know how it was carried and I'll tell you what's most likely.
Not sure how the movers carried it, I wasn't watching. Maybe on its back in the van? Compressor is running and the back is slightly warm. Do I switch it off then?

Yes. If there's a real chance it travelled on its back, I'd switch it off at the socket now and leave it standing upright overnight, ideally 12 to 24 hours, before switching it back on. If it was laid down, some compressor oil may have run into the thin cooling pipes. Running it can push that oil round where it partly blocks the refrigerant, so it cools poorly. Letting it stand gives the oil time to drain back into the compressor. Losing a day is a small price compared with risking the compressor. The good news is that it doesn't sound broken. The compressor is running and the back is slightly warm, which is exactly what you want to hear. At 3 hours, not being cold yet is still well within normal for a fridge freezer starting from warm, and the gurgling fits refrigerant settling after a move. In order of likelihood, here's what's going on:
1. Normal settling and pull-down time. This is most likely, and it'll be properly cold within a day of running.
2. Oil disturbed by being carried flat. Standing it upright, then restarting, usually sorts this. Most fridges come through it fine, even after a few hours of running.
3. A genuine fault. This is unlikely at this stage, because the compressor is starting and running. What to do:
1. Switch it off and leave it upright overnight with the doors shut. If you can find out from the movers that it stayed upright the whole way, you can switch it straight back on instead.
2. When you restart it, give it 6 to 12 hours for the fridge and up to 24 hours for the freezer, with no food in. If both get cold, nothing was wrong.
3. For tonight, keep anything perishable in cool bags with ice packs, or eat it first. There are a few warning signs that would point to a real fault. One is still no proper cooling after a full 24 hours of running following the rest. Another is the compressor clicking on and off every few minutes without settling into a steady hum. The last is a continuous loud hiss, or oily marks on the pipes at the back. If you see any of those, tell me and we'll work out whether it's the start relay or something that needs an engineer. In that case it's also worth raising with the removal company, as transit damage is usually something their insurance covers.
